7.1 — What horticulture includes
Theory
Understand the idea

Horticulture is the production of fruit, vegetables, nuts, flowers, turf and nursery plants. It includes food crops as well as plants grown for landscaping, gardens, recreation and sale through nurseries. Horticultural enterprises can differ greatly, so one example should not be treated as representing the whole industry.

Horticulture can be compared with broadacre cropping and livestock agriculture by considering land area, crop value and management intensity. Many horticultural crops are produced on smaller areas than broadacre crops, but they may require more concentrated labour, water, planning and monitoring. Some horticultural products may also have a relatively high value for the area used. These are general patterns, not rules that apply to every farm or crop.

The word intensive describes a system with concentrated inputs and management. It may involve frequent monitoring, careful water and nutrient management, skilled labour, pest and disease control, and detailed production planning. Intensive does not automatically mean that production occurs indoors. It also does not prove that a system is harmful, environmentally poor or better than another system. Its suitability depends on the crop, location, resources and management.

Common horticultural inputs include labour, water, nutrients, planting material, equipment, planning and information. Growers monitor plant growth, soil or growing conditions, weather, pests, diseases and product quality. Monitoring helps identify changes and supports timely management decisions.

Water and nutrients must be managed because plants need suitable growing conditions, but requirements vary between crops and environments. Pest and disease management also requires planning and evidence rather than assumptions. Labour may be needed for tasks such as planting, monitoring, harvesting, sorting or preparing products for sale.

A fair comparison between horticulture and another agricultural system applies the same criteria to both. Students should identify the products being grown, the land and resources used, the level of management required and the evidence supporting each claim.

Key takeaways

Horticulture includes fruit, vegetables, nuts, flowers, turf and nursery plants.

Horticulture can be compared with other agriculture using land area, crop value and management intensity.

Intensive production uses concentrated inputs and management but is not automatically indoor, harmful or superior.

Labour, water, nutrients, pest and disease management, planning and monitoring are common horticultural inputs.

Knowledge check

Which group contains only horticultural products?
A. Wheat, cattle and wool
B. Fruit, vegetables and nursery plants
C. Sheep, timber and grain
D. Milk, eggs and cotton

Answer: B. Fruit, vegetables and nursery plants
Correct feedback: Correct. Fruit, vegetables and nursery plants are all included within horticulture.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening definition and identify the products specifically included in horticulture.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

What does management intensity describe?
A. The colour of the harvested product
B. The distance from a farm to a market
C. The concentration of inputs, planning and monitoring
D. The total number of plant species in Australia

Answer: C. The concentration of inputs, planning and monitoring
Correct feedback: Correct. Management intensity refers to how concentrated inputs, labour, planning and monitoring are.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on how much management and input are concentrated within the production system.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

How may horticulture differ from broadacre cropping?
A. It always uses more land
B. It may use smaller areas with more concentrated management
C. It never requires machinery
D. It produces only non-food plants

Answer: B. It may use smaller areas with more concentrated management
Correct feedback: Correct. Horticulture may use smaller areas while requiring concentrated labour, water and monitoring.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory presents general differences in land area and management, not absolute rules.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

What does intensive horticulture automatically mean?
A. Production must occur indoors
B. The system is environmentally harmful
C. The system is superior to all alternatives
D. Inputs and management are concentrated

Answer: D. Inputs and management are concentrated
Correct feedback: Correct. Intensive describes concentrated inputs and management, not a judgement about location or quality.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph defining intensive and separating it from unsupported assumptions.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which is a common input in horticultural production?
A. Water
B. Breed records
C. Livestock yards
D. Wool classing

Answer: A. Water
Correct feedback: Correct. Water is a common horticultural input that must be managed for plant growth.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose an input directly connected with growing and managing plants.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Why do horticultural growers monitor crops?
A. To guarantee that pests never occur
B. To identify changes and support management decisions
C. To make every crop grow at the same rate
D. To replace all planning

Answer: B. To identify changes and support management decisions
Correct feedback: Correct. Monitoring helps growers detect changes and make informed management decisions.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Monitoring provides evidence for decisions; it does not guarantee identical or problem-free crops.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which factor may require regular management in horticulture?
A. Water and nutrients
B. Animal pedigree
C. Wool fibre length
D. Livestock movement

Answer: A. Water and nutrients
Correct feedback: Correct. Water and nutrients are managed to support suitable plant-growing conditions.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on resources needed directly by plants during growth.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which statement about horticultural enterprises is most accurate?
A. Every enterprise uses the same land area
B. Every crop has identical resource needs
C. Enterprises vary in crops, scale, inputs and management
D. All horticulture produces food

Answer: C. Enterprises vary in crops, scale, inputs and management
Correct feedback: Correct. Horticultural enterprises differ greatly in their products, scale and management.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory warns against treating one horticultural example as representative of the whole industry.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

What makes a comparison between horticulture and livestock agriculture fair?
A. Using different criteria for each system
B. Applying the same criteria to both systems
C. Assuming horticulture is more valuable
D. Comparing only the strongest feature of horticulture

Answer: B. Applying the same criteria to both systems
Correct feedback: Correct. Fair comparisons apply the same criteria to each agricultural system.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Consistent criteria are needed to avoid a biased comparison.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which conclusion is best supported by the theory?
A. Intensive horticulture is always better
B. Horticulture always produces more value than livestock farming
C. All horticulture occurs on small farms
D. System suitability depends on crops, resources, location and management

Answer: D. System suitability depends on crops, resources, location and management
Correct feedback: Correct. Suitability depends on the particular production context rather than the system label alone.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Avoid universal claims and consider the interacting conditions described in the theory.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Written evidence

Prompt: Compare horticulture with either broadacre cropping or livestock agriculture using land area, product value and management intensity.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Horticulture may use a smaller land area than broadacre cropping but can require more concentrated labour, water, planning and monitoring. Some horticultural crops may also have a relatively high value for the area used. These are general patterns, so a fair comparison must consider the particular crop, location and management system.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Prompt: Explain what intensive horticulture means and identify three inputs or management activities it may involve.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Intensive horticulture means that inputs and management are concentrated. It may involve careful water and nutrient management, frequent crop monitoring and planned pest or disease control. The term does not automatically mean that production is indoors, harmful or better than another system.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Source boundary

Teach  horticulture through its products, inputs and general production characteristics. Do not provide current statistics, local operating procedures or universal claims about land use, crop value, environmental impact or superiority. Any practical activity or local production context must be confirmed by the teacher.

Sources

Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

7.2 — Why crops suit particular regions
Theory
Understand the idea

Different crops grow best under different combinations of environmental and management conditions. Crop suitability depends on several interacting factors rather than one feature alone. Important factors include climate, temperature, water availability, soil properties, sunlight, season length, infrastructure and management.

Climate influences rainfall, temperature patterns and seasonal conditions that affect plant growth. Temperature can influence how well a crop develops, while sunlight provides the energy needed for photosynthesis. Water is essential for plant growth, but reliable water alone does not guarantee success. Soil properties such as drainage, texture and fertility also influence how well plants grow, and suitable management is needed to respond to changing conditions.

Infrastructure can affect crop suitability because growers need practical ways to transport, store and market their produce. Roads, irrigation systems, processing facilities and other services may support production, but they work together with environmental conditions rather than replacing them. Management decisions, planning and monitoring also influence how successfully a crop can be grown.

Examples of recognised Australian horticultural regions include the Goulburn Valley, the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, Sunraysia, Riverland, northern Tasmania, south-west Western Australia and coastal northern New South Wales and Queensland. These regions are useful examples because they support different horticultural industries. However, they should not be treated as places where only one crop can grow or where success is guaranteed.

A reasoned location claim connects the needs of a crop with evidence about a particular place. For example, a student might compare climate, available water, soil properties, season length and infrastructure before deciding whether a location may suit a crop. A stronger explanation uses several linked factors rather than relying on one feature alone.

Good agricultural comparisons explain both the evidence supporting a claim and the limits of that evidence. Different crops have different requirements, and conditions can change over time. For this reason, conclusions should be based on multiple factors and expressed carefully rather than as absolute statements.

Key takeaways

Crop suitability depends on several interacting environmental and management factors.

Water availability is important but does not guarantee successful crop production.

Australian horticultural regions are useful examples, not exclusive growing areas.

Strong location claims link crop needs with evidence from several factors.

Knowledge check

Which factor is part of crop suitability?
A. Climate
B. Product packaging
C. Advertising slogans
D. Farm logos

Answer: A. Climate
Correct feedback: Correct. Climate is one of several important factors affecting crop suitability.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph and identify the environmental and management factors.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Why is water availability alone not enough to guarantee success?
A. Other factors such as soil, climate and management also matter
B. Water is never important for crops
C. All crops require identical conditions
D. Infrastructure replaces environmental conditions

Answer: A. Other factors such as soil, climate and management also matter
Correct feedback: Correct. Successful crop production depends on several interacting factors.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory explains that water works together with other environmental and management factors.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which soil characteristic may influence crop growth?
A. Drainage
B. Package colour
C. Market advertising
D. Product label design

Answer: A. Drainage
Correct feedback: Correct. Drainage is one of the soil properties that can influence plant growth.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Look for the examples of soil properties listed in the theory.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Why can infrastructure influence crop suitability?
A. It can support transport, storage and marketing
B. It replaces the need for sunlight
C. It guarantees crop success
D. It changes the climate

Answer: A. It can support transport, storage and marketing
Correct feedback: Correct. Infrastructure supports production but does not replace environmental conditions.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on how infrastructure supports the movement and handling of produce.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

What is true about recognised Australian horticultural regions?
A. They are examples of horticultural regions, not guarantees for only one crop
B. Each region grows only one horticultural product
C. Every region has identical growing conditions
D. They guarantee success for every crop

Answer: A. They are examples of horticultural regions, not guarantees for only one crop
Correct feedback: Correct. These regions are examples and should not be treated as exclusive growing areas.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory warns against treating example regions as guarantees.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which combination provides the strongest evidence for a location claim?
A. Climate, soil properties, water and infrastructure
B. One factor on its own
C. A product advertisement
D. The popularity of a crop

Answer: A. Climate, soil properties, water and infrastructure
Correct feedback: Correct. Strong claims combine several relevant factors rather than relying on one.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. A reasoned claim links multiple factors to the crop's needs.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Why is season length important?
A. It can influence how well a crop completes its growth
B. It determines the packaging used
C. It replaces soil properties
D. It guarantees higher crop value

Answer: A. It can influence how well a crop completes its growth
Correct feedback: Correct. Season length is one of the environmental factors affecting crop suitability.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the list of interacting factors in the opening paragraph.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

What should a reasoned location claim include?
A. Evidence linking crop needs with features of the place
B. Only the name of the region
C. A guarantee that the crop will succeed
D. One environmental factor without explanation

Answer: A. Evidence linking crop needs with features of the place
Correct feedback: Correct. A strong claim explains how the location matches the crop's requirements.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Think about how crop needs should be connected with evidence from the location.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Why should conclusions about crop suitability be expressed carefully?
A. Conditions and crop requirements can vary
B. Every crop grows equally well everywhere
C. Climate never changes
D. Infrastructure always determines success

Answer: A. Conditions and crop requirements can vary
Correct feedback: Correct. Conditions vary, so conclusions should avoid absolute statements.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the final paragraph about evidence and changing conditions.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which statement best matches the theory?
A. Crop suitability depends on interacting factors rather than one condition
B. Water alone determines where every crop grows
C. One recognised region is always the best location
D. Management has no influence on crop production

Answer: A. Crop suitability depends on interacting factors rather than one condition
Correct feedback: Correct. Crop suitability results from the interaction of several environmental and management factors.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory repeatedly emphasises that no single factor determines suitability.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Written evidence

Prompt: Explain why a crop may suit one Australian region by linking at least four factors from the theory to evidence about the place.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A crop may suit a region because its climate, temperature, available water, soil properties and season length match the crop's needs. Infrastructure can also support transport and marketing. A strong explanation links each factor with evidence instead of relying on only one condition such as water availability.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Prompt: Compare two recognised horticultural regions by discussing the factors that could influence crop suitability without claiming either region guarantees success.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Both regions can be compared using climate, soil properties, water availability, sunlight, season length, infrastructure and management. The evidence may suggest that different crops could suit each region, but no conclusion should claim that one crop can grow only there or that success is guaranteed.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Source boundary

Teach  crop suitability through interacting environmental and management factors using recognised Australian horticultural regions as examples only. Do not provide current production statistics, rankings, local growing instructions or claims that any single factor guarantees success.

Sources

7.3 — Seasonality, markets and production decisions
Theory
Understand the idea

Seasonal production occurs because crop growth and harvest timing respond to biological needs and environmental conditions. Temperature, rainfall, sunlight, water availability and season length can affect when a crop develops, matures and is ready to harvest. Different crops respond differently, so seasonal patterns are not identical across all products or regions.

After harvest, horticultural products move through a supply chain. Domestic markets are destinations within Australia, while export markets are destinations in other countries. These markets may involve different transport distances, delivery times, quality expectations, packaging needs and buyer requirements. A market choice is therefore part of production planning, not simply a decision made after the crop is harvested.

Perishability is important because many horticultural products can lose quality over time. Growers and supply-chain businesses must consider how quickly a product needs to reach buyers and what transport, storage and handling arrangements are available. A less perishable product may allow different market choices from a product that must move quickly.

Timing can influence whether produce reaches a market when buyers want it. Seasonal availability may also influence price and product quality, but it cannot guarantee either. Prices can be affected by supply, demand, competition, buyer requirements and other changing conditions. Quality also depends on crop condition, harvest timing, handling, storage and transport.

A production decision should be analysed using evidence, constraints and trade-offs. Evidence may include seasonal conditions, expected harvest timing, transport access and buyer requirements. Constraints are limits such as perishability, distance, infrastructure or available labour. A trade-off occurs when one choice creates an advantage in one area but a cost or limitation in another. For example, reaching a more distant market may provide another sales opportunity but require longer transport and stricter quality control.

A defensible decision explains the context, uses relevant evidence and acknowledges uncertainty. It should not assume that one market, harvest time or production choice is always best.

Key takeaways

Seasonal production is shaped by crop biology and environmental conditions.

Domestic and export markets are different destinations within a supply chain.

Perishability, quality, timing, transport and buyer requirements influence production decisions.

Strong decisions use evidence, identify constraints and explain trade-offs.

Knowledge check

What causes seasonal production patterns?
A. Crop biology and environmental conditions
B. Packaging colour alone
C. The name of the market
D. A fixed rule for every crop

Answer: A. Crop biology and environmental conditions
Correct feedback: Correct. Seasonal production responds to biological needs and conditions such as temperature, rainfall and sunlight.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph and identify what affects crop growth and harvest timing.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

What is a domestic market?
A. A market within Australia
B. A market in another country
C. A storage facility only
D. A type of crop disease

Answer: A. A market within Australia
Correct feedback: Correct. Domestic markets are destinations within Australia.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the destination of the product within the supply chain.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

What is an export market?
A. A market in another country
B. A market only at the farm gate
C. A market that never uses transport
D. A market for one crop only

Answer: A. A market in another country
Correct feedback: Correct. Export markets are destinations outside Australia.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph distinguishing domestic and export destinations.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Why does perishability affect market choice?
A. Some products can lose quality over time
B. It guarantees a higher price
C. It removes the need for transport
D. It makes every buyer requirement identical

Answer: A. Some products can lose quality over time
Correct feedback: Correct. Perishable products may need faster transport and carefully managed storage and handling.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Consider what can happen to product quality as time passes.
Source: Authorised Module 7 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1wRaaHybkaG_WA0zyvCCm_Ub5yVXOtjyHM4IfM-Ed6RA/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Australian horticulture: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/farm-food-drought/hort-policy

Which factor may influence whether produce reaches buyers at a suitable time?
A. Harvest and transport timing
B. Farm logo design
C. The spelling of the crop name
D. The colour of machinery

Answer: A. Harvest and transport timing
Correct feedback: Correct. Harvest and transport timing affect when produce reaches the market.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose the factor directly connected with when the product is available to buyers.

What can seasonal availability influence without guaranteeing?
A. Price and quality
B. The identity of the crop
C. The location of every buyer
D. The exact transport route

Answer: A. Price and quality
Correct feedback: Correct. Seasonal availability may influence price and quality, but other factors also affect both.

Which is an example of a buyer requirement?
A. A specified product quality
B. The region's annual rainfall
C. The crop's biological growth cycle
D. The colour of the soil

Answer: A. A specified product quality
Correct feedback: Correct. Buyers may set requirements for product quality, timing, packaging or delivery.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on a condition requested by the person or business purchasing the product.

What is a constraint in a production decision?
A. A limit such as distance, perishability or available labour
B. Evidence that guarantees success
C. A claim that one market is always best
D. A benefit with no disadvantage

Answer: A. A limit such as distance, perishability or available labour
Correct feedback: Correct. Constraints are limits that affect which choices are practical.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph defining evidence, constraints and trade-offs.

What is a trade-off?
A. A choice that creates an advantage and a cost or limitation
B. A decision with no disadvantages
C. A current market ranking
D. A guarantee of product quality

Answer: A. A choice that creates an advantage and a cost or limitation
Correct feedback: Correct. A trade-off involves gaining something in one area while accepting a cost or limitation elsewhere.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Think about how one production choice can have both benefits and drawbacks.

A. It uses evidence, explains context and acknowledges uncertainty
B. It assumes the most distant market is best

Answer: A. It uses evidence, explains context and acknowledges uncertainty
Correct feedback: Correct. A defensible decision connects evidence to the context and recognises what remains uncertain.

Written evidence

Prompt: Analyse a horticultural production decision by identifying evidence, two constraints and one trade-off.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A grower considering a distant market could use evidence about harvest timing, product perishability, transport access and buyer requirements. Constraints may include the time the product can maintain quality and the available transport infrastructure. A trade-off is that the distant market may offer another sales opportunity, but it also requires longer transport and more careful quality control.

Prompt: Explain why seasonal availability may influence price and quality but cannot guarantee either.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Seasonal availability can change how much produce reaches a market and when it arrives. However, price also depends on supply, demand, competition and buyer requirements. Quality depends on crop condition, harvest timing, handling, storage and transport. Therefore, seasonality is only one influence and cannot guarantee a particular price or quality result.

Source boundary

Teach  seasonality, market destinations and production decisions conceptually. Do not provide current market rankings, exhaustive export destinations, price predictions, farm-specific marketing advice or claims that seasonal availability guarantees price or quality.
